questions.stem: An events coordinator has four requests from colleagues and an hour to spare before a busy week. She wants to start with the one that is a good fit for Claude as long as she gives the result an ordinary read-through, with no specialist sign-off needed. Which request BEST fits that description?

options.text: Draft the wording of the refund terms that customers must accept before they can buy a ticket to the annual conference.
Write the allergen and dietary information that will be printed on the menu cards for the conference dinner.
Brainstorm twenty theme ideas and session titles for an internal team offsite, for the planning group to shortlist.
Decide which of the forty speaker applicants should be accepted for the main stage based on their submitted bios.

questions.explanation: Brainstorming themes for an internal offsite is low-stakes. A wrong idea costs nothing, any weak idea is easy to spot, and people choose from the list before anything is used. That is the classic good-fit task. The other three either create legal commitments, carry health risk, or make decisions about people, so they need specialist review or a human decision-maker.

whyWrong.A: Refund terms that customers accept are a legal commitment. Claude can draft them, but legal or the policy owner must review them before use. An ordinary read-through is not enough.
whyWrong.B: Allergen information printed for guests is a health-and-safety statement where an error can hurt someone. It must come from the caterer's verified data and be checked, not drafted from Claude's general knowledge.
whyWrong.D: Accepting or rejecting applicants is a decision about people. Claude can summarize bios against stated criteria, but a person on the program committee has to make and own each decision.

questions.mindset: Ask 'if this is wrong, who gets hurt?' Low harm plus a human choosing from the output means good fit.

questions.stem: A busy account manager is behind on his mandatory annual data-protection training. The module ends with a graded quiz, and the company's learning policy says employees must complete assessments themselves. He asks whether he can paste the quiz questions into Claude and submit its answers to save time. What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.text: No. The quiz must reflect his own understanding, so he should take it himself, and he can use Claude beforehand to explain the training material.
Yes, provided he reads each answer Claude gives and only submits the ones that he personally agrees are correct.
Yes, because the training is internal and low risk, so using Claude to complete it does not harm customers or the company.
Yes, provided he first asks Claude to confirm that using it on an internal training quiz is permitted under the policy.

questions.explanation: The learning policy requires employees to complete assessments themselves, and the quiz exists to verify that he personally understands data protection. Submitting Claude's answers would misrepresent his own work and defeat the purpose of the training. Claude still has a legitimate role here: explaining the concepts beforehand so he learns the material faster and then takes the quiz himself.

whyWrong.B: Agreeing with an answer is not the same as producing it. The policy requires his own completion, so skimming Claude's answers still breaks the rule and defeats the purpose of the quiz.
whyWrong.C: 'It's internal' does not make a policy breach acceptable. An employee who has not learned data protection is exactly the kind of risk the training is there to reduce.
whyWrong.D: Claude cannot authorize its own use or interpret your company's policy for you. The policy is already clear, and if it were not, the question would go to the policy owner.

questions.mindset: Use Claude to learn, not to stand in for you where your own work is what is being assessed.

questions.stem: A small e-commerce brand is launching a new skincare line and has no customer feedback yet. The marketing lead asks Claude to write thirty five-star reviews, each in a different customer voice with first names and cities, to post on the product page at launch. What should the marketer do?

options.text: Go ahead, but ask Claude to keep every review realistic and moderate so that none of them makes exaggerated claims about results.
Go ahead, but add a small note under the reviews saying some content on the page may have been prepared with AI assistance.
Go ahead, but have the product team check every review so that it only describes features that the product really has.
Decline this request, and instead use Claude to draft honest launch copy and a follow-up email inviting real buyers to leave reviews.

questions.explanation: Reviews attributed to customers who do not exist are deceptive: they mislead buyers into thinking thirty real people bought and rated the product, and fabricated testimonials of this kind breach consumer-protection rules in many places. No wording change, fact check or footnote fixes that, because the deception is the whole point of the content. The legitimate goal — social proof — can be met by collecting genuine reviews, and Claude can help with that honest version.

whyWrong.A: Moderate wording does not change the core problem: the reviewers do not exist. Toning down the claims only makes the fake reviews more convincing.
whyWrong.B: A vague footnote does not make invented customers honest. Readers would still believe that thirty real people bought and rated the product.
whyWrong.C: Checking features for accuracy misses the point. The deception is in who the reviews claim to come from, not in what they say about the product.

questions.mindset: If the content only works by deceiving people, no safeguard rescues it; redirect to the honest version of the goal.

questions.stem: A credit union's lending team receives about 200 small-business loan applications a month. A team lead proposes uploading each application to the approved Claude workspace and letting Claude return 'approve' or 'decline', which officers would then send out, so the backlog clears faster. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Adopt the proposal, but ask Claude in the prompt to explain its reasoning for each approve or decline so that officers can read it later.
Have Claude summarize each application against the credit union's written lending criteria and flag gaps, with an officer making every decision.
Adopt the proposal for applications under a set amount, where the financial risk to the credit union is small enough to accept errors.
Stop using Claude in lending completely, because financial decisions are too sensitive for any kind of AI assistance in the process.

questions.explanation: Approving or declining credit is a consequential decision about people and businesses, so a qualified officer has to make and own each decision rather than send out an AI's verdict. Redesigning the task keeps most of the time saving: Claude organizes the evidence against the credit union's own written criteria and points out missing documents, and the loan officer decides. That is the standard pattern for high-stakes decisions: Claude prepares, a qualified human decides.

whyWrong.A: An explanation officers 'can read later' is not review. Claude would still be making the decision, and the officers would just be sending it out.
whyWrong.C: The small loan size lowers the risk to the credit union, not to the applicant. A wrongly declined business is harmed whatever the amount, and the decision still needs a human.
whyWrong.D: A blanket ban throws away a safe, useful assist. Assisted preparation with human decision-making is appropriate, so redesigning beats abandoning.

questions.mindset: For decisions about people, Claude prepares the evidence; a qualified human makes the call.

questions.stem: A secondary-school teacher has 150 history essays to mark before report cards are due. She wants to give each essay to Claude along with the rubric, have Claude assign the final grade, and paste those grades straight into the school's reporting system so she can focus on lesson planning. What is the BEST way for her to use Claude here?

options.text: Use the proposal as planned, but run every essay through Claude twice and only accept a grade when both runs agree with each other.
Use the proposal as planned, and tell students and parents in the course newsletter that grading this term was carried out with AI help.
Have Claude draft rubric-based feedback and a suggested band for each essay, then read the essays and set every final grade herself.
Avoid Claude for anything grade-related and use it only for lesson planning, since grades are too sensitive to involve AI in at all.

questions.explanation: Grades affect students' records and opportunities, so the teacher should read the work and own every final grade. Claude can still save hours by drafting rubric-aligned comments and a suggested band for each essay, which she accepts, adjusts or rejects as she reads. She also catches cases where Claude has misjudged an unusual but strong argument — exactly the kind of subjective, high-stakes judgment that needs a qualified human reviewer.

whyWrong.A: Two runs agreeing shows consistency, not correctness. Claude can be confidently wrong the same way twice, and no qualified person has reviewed the grade.
whyWrong.B: Disclosure is important, but it does not replace review. Telling parents AI was used does not make an unreviewed grade fair or accurate.
whyWrong.D: Banning AI from assessment work gives up a safe, useful assist. Drafting feedback with teacher review is an appropriate, efficient use.

questions.mindset: Disclosure and consistency checks are add-ons; the qualified human still owns any judgment about a person.

questions.stem: A regional news website wants to turn the dozens of press releases it receives each day into short news items. The digital editor proposes having Claude rewrite each release into a 150-word article that publishes automatically to the site, so the small team can focus on original reporting. Which TWO safeguards should the newsroom put in place for this to be an appropriate use? Choose TWO.

options.text: An editor reads and checks each item against the source release, and against other sources where needed, before it is published.
The prompt instructs Claude to double-check every fact in the release itself and to omit any claim it is not fully confident about.
The workflow switches to the most capable Claude model so that the rewritten articles contain fewer errors and need less checking.
Readers are told, in line with the outlet's editorial policy, that AI was used to help produce these items.
Each article ends with a standard line stating that the content is based on a press release and may not be fully accurate.

questions.explanation: Content published to the public under the outlet's name needs editorial control before it goes out, and readers deserve to know how it was produced. An editor checking each item against the source release (and other sources where needed) catches fabricated or distorted details, and disclosing AI involvement keeps the outlet's relationship with its readers honest. Together these turn an unattended pipeline into an assisted workflow the newsroom can stand behind.

whyWrong.B: Asking Claude to check itself is not a control. Claude can be confidently wrong, and its own confidence is not a reliable signal of accuracy.
whyWrong.C: A stronger model may make fewer errors, but not zero, and press releases are often one-sided or incomplete. Editorial judgment is still needed before publication.
whyWrong.E: An 'it may not be accurate' line shifts the work of checking onto readers. A disclaimer does not replace editorial review, and it does not tell readers AI was involved.

questions.mindset: Public-facing content needs two things together: qualified human review before publication and honest disclosure of AI involvement.

questions.stem: A paralegal at a mid-sized firm wants to use Claude to prepare first drafts of standard mutual non-disclosure agreements for business clients, which currently take her about an hour each. The firm's AI policy allows client work in its approved workspace. Which TWO steps would MOST make this an appropriate use? Choose TWO.

options.text: Add a footer to every draft stating that the agreement was generated by AI and should be read carefully before signing.
Give Claude the firm's own approved NDA template and clause library to work from, rather than having it write from general knowledge.
Ask Claude at the end of each draft to confirm that the agreement is enforceable in the client's jurisdiction before it is sent.
Use the most capable model for every NDA so that the drafts are legally sound enough to go to clients without further review.
Have a supervising attorney review and approve each draft before it reaches the client, as with any paralegal work product.

questions.explanation: Legal documents sent to clients are high-stakes output, so a qualified professional — the supervising attorney — must review and approve each draft before it goes out, just as with any paralegal work product. Grounding Claude in the firm's own approved template and clause library cuts the chance of invented or unsuitable terms and makes the attorney's review faster. Together these keep the time saving while keeping the firm accountable.

whyWrong.A: A footer warning shifts the risk onto the client. It does not replace the attorney review the firm owes its clients.
whyWrong.C: Claude cannot certify enforceability. Its confirmation is just more generated text, and a lawyer must make that judgment.
whyWrong.D: No model choice removes the need for professional review of legal work. A bigger model is a quality lever, not a governance control.

questions.mindset: Ground the draft in approved sources, then have a qualified professional sign off.

questions.stem: An HR coordinator must prepare final-pay statements for twelve employees leaving after a restructuring. Each statement includes unused leave, notice pay and deductions under local rules. She is considering asking Claude to calculate every figure from a description of each person's situation, because the payroll team is overloaded this week. What is the MOST appropriate use of Claude?

options.text: Let Claude calculate all of the figures, then ask it to recheck its own arithmetic carefully before she sends the statements out.
Let Claude calculate all of the figures, and add a note to each statement inviting employees to report any error they spot.
Let Claude calculate all of the figures, provided that she first gives it a copy of the local employment rules to use as reference.
Take the figures from the payroll system and payroll team, and use Claude to draft the clear cover letter that explains each item.

questions.explanation: Final-pay figures are legal entitlements that must be exactly right, and language models can slip on precise arithmetic and rule application even when they sound confident. That work belongs to the system of record and the people accountable for payroll. Claude is a good fit for the part where its strengths matter: turning verified figures into a clear, respectful explanation for each employee. A deadline does not change who owns the numbers.

whyWrong.A: Self-checking is not verification. Claude can repeat the same mistake, and an employee's legal entitlement should not depend on it.
whyWrong.B: Asking departing employees to find the errors puts the burden on the people harmed. It is not a safeguard.
whyWrong.C: Supplying the rules helps, but Claude would still be the one calculating zero-tolerance figures with no system of record or accountable reviewer.

questions.mindset: Zero-tolerance numbers come from the system of record; Claude explains them, it does not produce them.

questions.stem: A water utility wants to add a Claude-powered assistant to its website to answer customer questions about billing dates, payment options and outage updates. The customer-service manager is drafting the requirements before handing the build to the company's developers. Which TWO requirements are MOST important for this to be an appropriate customer-facing use? Choose TWO.

options.text: The assistant clearly tells customers they are talking with an AI system, not a human service agent.
The assistant is given a friendly human name and personality so that customers feel they are getting personal service.
Disputed bills, hardship requests and shut-off questions are handed to a human agent rather than answered by the assistant.
The assistant's prompt tells it never to make mistakes and to always give customers the most favorable answer possible.
The assistant runs on the most capable model available so that it can resolve every type of request without human staff.

questions.explanation: Customers should never be left believing they are chatting with a person when they are talking to software: clear AI disclosure is a basic transparency safeguard for any customer-facing assistant. And requests that affect a customer's money or an essential service — billing disputes, hardship arrangements, shut-offs — are consequential and should go to a person who can be held accountable. Routine FAQs stay with the assistant, which is where the efficiency comes from.

whyWrong.B: A friendly name is fine, but presenting the assistant so customers think it is a person conflicts with the disclosure safeguard.
whyWrong.D: 'Never make mistakes' is a wish, not a control, and 'always the most favorable answer' would create commitments the utility cannot honor.
whyWrong.E: Model capability does not remove the need for human handling of high-impact cases. Removing staff entirely is the opposite of the safeguard needed.

questions.mindset: Customer-facing AI must say it is AI, and high-impact cases need a human route.

questions.stem: An insurance claims team writes about forty claim-denial letters a week. Each letter must cite the specific policy clause and explain the customer's appeal rights. A team leader wants to save time with Claude but is unsure whether this work is appropriate for it. Which approach BEST balances efficiency with responsible use?

options.text: Use Claude to write the letters from the adjuster's short summary, and send them under the team's name without review to cut the backlog.
Use Claude to draft each letter from the claim file and policy wording, with the responsible adjuster checking and signing it before it is sent.
Keep writing these letters by hand, since any letter that denies a customer's claim is too consequential to involve AI at any point.
Use Claude to draft each letter, and include a sentence telling the customer the letter was AI-generated and could contain mistakes.

questions.explanation: Denial letters affect a customer's money and legal rights, and each one must cite specific policy language — exactly the kind of detail a language model can get subtly wrong or invent. Drafting from the actual claim file and policy wording keeps Claude grounded, and the responsible adjuster checks the clause citation and appeal-rights wording before signing. The team keeps the time saving and a qualified person stays accountable for what is sent.

whyWrong.A: Sending without review means a cited clause or appeal right could be wrong or invented, with direct harm to the customer and legal exposure for the insurer.
whyWrong.C: A ban gives up a safe efficiency gain. Drafting with qualified review is an appropriate, safeguarded use.
whyWrong.D: Telling the customer the letter may be wrong does not make it right. Disclosure accompanies review; it does not replace it.

questions.mindset: In high-risk areas, the usual answer is 'Claude drafts from real sources, a qualified person signs'.

questions.stem: A subscription software company sets up an automated process in which Claude writes replies to routine customer emails and sends them without a person reading them first. To make the replies feel personal, the support manager wants each one signed 'Sarah, Customer Success Team', although no Sarah exists. Leadership asks for the MOST appropriate change before the process goes live.

options.text: Keep the Sarah signature, but have Claude vary the wording of each reply so that customers do not notice that the messages are automated.
Keep the Sarah signature, but add a feedback link to each reply so that unhappy customers can ask to speak with a manager.
Sign the replies as an AI assistant on behalf of the support team, and give customers an easy way to reach a real person.
Keep the Sarah signature, but have a supervisor spot-check a random sample of the replies each week for tone and accuracy.

questions.explanation: Signing automated replies with an invented human name presents AI output as human-written. That deception — not the tone or the repetitive phrasing — is the problem leadership needs to fix. Signing as an AI assistant keeps the efficiency while telling customers the truth, and an easy route to a real person protects anyone whose issue turns out not to be routine. Spot-checks and feedback links are useful additions, but they leave the false identity in place.

whyWrong.A: Varying the wording to hide automation makes the deception worse. The problem is the false identity, not repetitive phrasing.
whyWrong.B: A feedback link helps unhappy customers, but every customer is still being told that a person named Sarah wrote to them.
whyWrong.D: Spot-checking improves quality, but it does nothing about the false claim that a human wrote each reply.

questions.mindset: Never let AI output pose as a person; honest labeling plus a human route keeps both trust and efficiency.

questions.stem: A department head, worried about leaks before a reorganization, asks an operations analyst to export the team's chat messages and have Claude give every employee a 'loyalty and trustworthiness score' from 1 to 10, to decide who is briefed early. The company workspace is approved for internal data. What should the analyst do?

options.text: Decline to produce individual trustworthiness scores, and raise the request with HR or compliance so they can decide how to handle the leak concern.
Produce the scores, but replace employee names with ID numbers first so that Claude's assessments are not biased by who wrote each message.
Produce the scores, but ask Claude to apply the same neutral criteria to every person and to list the messages behind each score it gives.
Produce the scores in the approved workspace, since internal data is permitted there and the scores would only be seen by the department head.

questions.explanation: Scoring individual employees for 'loyalty and trustworthiness' by mining their chat messages is covert profiling of people. It raises serious privacy and employment-law concerns regardless of which tool or workspace is used, and an approved workspace makes the data location acceptable, not the purpose. The right move is to decline the scoring and route the genuine concern — leak risk before a reorganization — to the people who own it: HR or compliance.

whyWrong.B: Pseudonymizing the input does nothing about the purpose. The scores would still be mapped back to real people and used to judge them.
whyWrong.C: Consistent criteria and cited messages make the profiling look more rigorous, but they do not make an inappropriate use acceptable.
whyWrong.D: Approval of the workspace covers where data may go, not every purpose. Being seen by only one person does not change what is being done to employees.

questions.mindset: An approved tool does not approve every purpose; some uses are off-limits however carefully they are done.

questions.stem: A hospital outpatient department receives hundreds of non-urgent messages a week through its patient portal, for example 'Can I take my usual allergy tablet before my scan?'. The nurse manager wants to use the hospital's approved Claude deployment to speed up replies. Which TWO elements should the workflow include to make this an appropriate use? Choose TWO.

options.text: Claude sends replies straight to patients for questions that it classifies as routine, and passes anything else to the nursing team.
Each reply ends with a line stating that the message is general information and is not a substitute for medical advice.
A registered nurse reviews, edits and approves every Claude-drafted reply before it is sent to the patient.
Patients are told, in line with hospital policy, that AI helps the care team draft replies to portal messages.
The prompt tells Claude to be cautious and to recommend calling the clinic whenever it has any uncertainty about a question.

questions.explanation: Replies that give medical guidance to patients are high-stakes output. The two safeguards that make the workflow appropriate are a qualified clinician — a registered nurse — reviewing, editing and approving every reply before it is sent, and transparency with patients that AI helps draft the responses. With both in place, Claude speeds up drafting while the care team stays accountable for every answer.

whyWrong.A: Letting Claude decide which questions are 'routine' and then reply on its own removes the clinician from exactly the decisions that need one. A misjudged 'routine' question could harm a patient.
whyWrong.B: A 'not medical advice' line on a reply that gives medical guidance is a disclaimer, not a safeguard. It does not replace clinical review.
whyWrong.E: Telling Claude to be cautious is a prompt instruction, not a control. Claude can be confidently wrong without signaling any uncertainty.

questions.mindset: For health advice: a qualified clinician approves every reply, and patients know AI helped.

questions.stem: A procurement specialist, a non-technical Associate-level user, has found that Claude is very good at spotting unusual clauses in supplier contracts. She now wants every contract that arrives in the shared inbox to be read automatically, given a risk rating by Claude, and filed with no one looking at it, and she plans to build this herself over a weekend. What is the MOST appropriate next step?

options.text: Build the automation herself as planned, since Claude has performed well on her manual tests and the ratings only feed an internal filing process.
Build the automation herself, but write a stricter prompt asking Claude to rate every contract as high risk whenever it has any doubt about a clause.
Drop the idea altogether, because contract review is legal work and only lawyers should ever be involved in assessing supplier agreements.
Keep using Claude for clause review with her own judgment on each contract, and take the automation idea to developers or architects and legal to design.

questions.explanation: Her current use — Claude flagging clauses while she reviews each contract — is appropriate and valuable. The proposed change removes all human review from a legal-risk process and needs intake integration, error handling and governance decisions; that design work belongs with developers or Claude Architects, with legal input, not a weekend build by an Associate. The Associate role is explicitly defined as recognizing limitations and escalating more complex or technical implementations, so escalating here keeps the benefit while putting the automated pipeline in the right hands.

whyWrong.A: Good results on a few manual tests do not justify unreviewed automation. Unread contracts filed with a wrong rating could hide real legal exposure.
whyWrong.B: A stricter prompt is still a prompt-only fix. It does not add a human checkpoint or address the integration and governance work required.
whyWrong.C: Dropping the idea discards a proven, appropriate use. Claude-assisted clause review with a human decision is fine; only the unreviewed automation is the problem.

questions.mindset: Know where your role stops: keep the safe assisted use, and escalate automated pipelines to builders.

questions.stem: A volunteer coordinator for a local election campaign has bought a dataset with each registered voter's browsing interests, purchase history and past turnout. She wants Claude to write a separate persuasive message for each of 5,000 voters, tailored to that person's individual profile. Which response is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Proceed, but have a campaign staffer read through a sample of the generated messages before sending to make sure that none of them are untrue.
Decline the profile-based targeting, and use Claude instead to draft accurate, general explainers of the candidate's positions for the campaign to review.
Proceed, but remove voters' names from the dataset before uploading it so that Claude only sees the interests and turnout data for each person.
Proceed, but tell Claude in the prompt that every message must stay factual and must not exaggerate the candidate's record in any way at all.

questions.explanation: The request combines purchased personal profiles (browsing interests, purchase history) with individually tailored political persuasion at scale. That raises data-sensitivity and consent problems with the dataset itself and uses it to micro-target persuasion — an inappropriate use regardless of how factual the messages are, because the method, not the wording, is the problem. Claude can still support the campaign legitimately with accurate, general explainers of the candidate's positions that the campaign reviews before use.

whyWrong.A: Spot-checking for falsehoods misses the issue. Even fully accurate messages built from individual voter profiles are individually targeted persuasion built on purchased personal data.
whyWrong.C: Removing names while keeping each person's detailed interest and turnout profile still produces individually targeted persuasion — and profiles like these can often be re-identified anyway.
whyWrong.D: A 'stay factual' instruction addresses truthfulness, not the targeting method or the data it relies on. A prompt cannot make the use appropriate.

questions.mindset: When the method itself is the problem, fixing the wording is not enough; switch to a legitimate way of meeting the goal.
